questions.stem: How does a key–value database store data?
options: As a pair consisting of a unique key and its associated value
As rows with dynamic columns grouped into families
As nodes and edges
As nested JSON documents queried by field
As immutable events in a chronological log
questions.explanation: Key–value databases store data as a unique key that serves as an identifier and a value that contains the data itself, eliminating structural complexity.

questions.stem: What is the primary goal of key–value databases?
options: Supporting complex joins across entities
Delivering ultra-fast lookups with minimal overhead
Enforcing relational integrity constraints
Enabling semantic reasoning over relationships
Providing rich ad-hoc analytical queries
questions.explanation: Key–value systems optimise for speed and scalability in workloads where the access pattern is simple and predictable rather than supporting complex queries.

questions.stem: Which forms can the value in a key–value database take?
options: Only fixed-length strings
Only numeric types
A simple string, a JSON object or even a binary blob
Only references to other keys
Only relational rows
questions.explanation: The value associated with a key can be a simple string, a JSON object or a binary blob; the database does not impose structure on it.

questions.stem: Which workloads are named as typical uses for key–value databases?
options: Regulatory reporting and cross-portfolio analytics
Fraud-ring detection and multi-hop traversal
Enterprise data warehousing
Caching, session management, token storage and high-volume read/write operations
Schema validation for partner integrations
questions.explanation: Key–value stores suit simple, predictable access patterns such as caching, session management, token storage and high-volume read/write operations.

questions.stem: In the loan approval example using Redis, what is used as the key and what does the value contain?
options: CustomerID as the key and a list of repayment dates as the value
OfficerID as the key and a branch name as the value
A composite of LoanID and RepayDate as the key and an amount as the value
Status as the key and a list of loans as the value
LoanID as the key and a JSON structure with LoanAmount, InterestRate, Status, CustomerID and OfficerID as the value
questions.explanation: The key is LoanID (for example L001) and the value is a JSON structure containing LoanAmount, InterestRate, Status, CustomerID and OfficerID, retrieved in a single lookup.

questions.stem: What response time is typical when a loan record is retrieved from a key–value cache in a single lookup?
options: Sub-millisecond latency
Several seconds
Around one minute
Batch-level latency of hours
The same latency as a multi-table relational join
questions.explanation: Because the entire record is fetched by key without querying a relational database or document store, the result is near-instant, often sub-millisecond latency.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT listed as a strength of key–value databases?
options: Extremely fast read and write performance
Support for ad-hoc queries beyond key retrieval
Simplicity of design and operation
Easy horizontal scaling
Suitability for caching layers in distributed architectures
questions.explanation: Key–value stores do not support ad-hoc queries beyond direct key retrieval; that is one of their main limitations.

questions.stem: How are key–value databases best understood within an enterprise architecture?
options: As the primary system of record for financial transactions
As replacements for relational databases
As performance accelerators that complement relational or document databases
As analytical engines for reporting
As the backbone for knowledge graphs
questions.explanation: Key–value databases are performance accelerators rather than full enterprise data platforms; they offload high-speed access needs, often as a caching layer beside primary storage.

questions.stem: In the comparison of relational and key–value models for loan approval, what is the key difference?
options: The relational model needs no joins while the key–value model needs many
The key–value model is normalised while the relational model is denormalised
The relational model is used only for caching
The relational model is structured and normalised with complex queries and joins, whereas the key–value model gives ultra-fast lookups with limited querying
Both models offer identical query flexibility
questions.explanation: The relational model stores the loan in a fact table joined to dimensions and supports complex queries; the key–value model stores a denormalised object retrievable in one lookup with limited querying.

questions.stem: Why is the key–value model described as the purest form of workload-driven data modelling?
options: Because it enforces the strictest schema of any NoSQL family
Because it supports every type of query
Because it is grounded in relational algebra
Because it stores relationships as first-class elements
Because it is optimised for simplicity and performance above all else
questions.explanation: The key–value model is unmatched in speed for direct lookups but too limited for relational integrity or analytics; it is optimised for simplicity and performance above everything.
